Rubin 's new PBS special shows you how to be happierhttp : **33;2771;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **34;2806;TOOLONG ... title= " Gretchen Rubin " alt= " Gretchen Rubin " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;2842;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 833645 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Science has finally caught up with what Bobby McFerrin told the tired , poor , huddled masses listening to the radio more than three decades ago . Don&amp;rsquo ; t worry , be happy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Even if the political landscape is a flaming dumpster fire , and the environment is careening into crisis mode . Don&amp;rsquo ; t worry , be happy . Author Gretchen Rubin says it&amp;rsquo ; s the psychological equivalent of putting on your oxygen mask first before helping others . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Sometimes people feel like it&amp;rsquo ; s selfish or not morally appropriate to seek to be happier . They think that with everything that&amp;rsquo ; s going on in the world , it seems very self-centered . But research shows that when we take steps to be happier and more calm and have more self-mastery in our own lives , we can turn outward and think about others&amp;rsquo ; problems and the problems of the world , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Often people who are unhappy become defensive and angry and preoccupied with their own problems . But when you&amp;rsquo ; re happy , you don&amp;rsquo ; t have to think about yourself as much and you have the emotional wherewithal to think about the pain of the world and the work of trying to help . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But how exactly do you go about implementing habits that will make you happier ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Rubin , who hosts a podcast and has written several best-selling books on the subject , including The Happiness Project and Happier at Home , has a theory . In her recent book The Four Tendencies &amp;mdash ; the basis of which is the subject of the PBS special Roadmap to Happiness With Gretchen Rubin &amp;mdash ; she lays out four personality types and the keys to spurring each to action . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; One of the big challenges of life is , how do we get ourselves to do the things we want to do ? And how do we get other people to do the things we want them to do ? The four tendencies make it much easier to understand why we do what we do , and why we don&amp;rsquo ; t , &amp;rdquo ; says Rubin. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;2872;TOOLONG ... title= " Roadmap to Happiness with Gretchen Rubin . PBS " alt= " Roadmap to Happiness with Gretchen Rubin . PBS " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;2908;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 833648 " /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In my own observation , people find it really useful and it explains things about themselves and other people that have been really mysterious . So there&amp;rsquo ; s a lot of satisfaction &amp;mdash ; like , &amp;lsquo ; Oh now I understand why I can&amp;rsquo ; t use a to-do list ! &amp;rsquo ; &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There&amp;rsquo ; s a quiz on Rubin&amp;rsquo ; s website you can take to determine your type . It all has to do with how we deal with the expectations others put on us , and the expectations we put on ourselves . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Upholders strive to meet both inner and outer expectations , meaning they don&amp;rsquo ; t want to let others or themselves down . Schedules and to-do lists work best for upholders &amp;mdash ; and Rubin admits she&amp;rsquo ; s a textbook case . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It made a lot of sense about a lot of things that had puzzled me my whole life became absolutely clear , &amp;rdquo ; she says , adding that pencilling in daily tasks helps her form habits . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I try hard to get enough sleep . I go for a walk or do yoga or do strength training just about every day . I try to read every day . I eat a very low-carb diet . I have all kinds of habits related to connecting with members of my family . I have a high affinity for habits and to-do lists . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Obligers , who comprise most of the population , make it a priority to meet outer expectations but not always inner ones . They&amp;rsquo ; ll put themselves last by default , and benefit from some form of external accountability . For example , if an obliger wants to exercise daily &amp;mdash ; an expectation they put on themselves &amp;mdash ; recruiting a workout buddy will help . Letting down a friend who&amp;rsquo ; s cleared their schedule is the last thing they&amp;rsquo ; d want to do . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Questioners , meanwhile , meet only inner expectations . In other words , they&amp;rsquo ; ll only do something if it makes sense to them and aligns with their values . They resist rules for rules&amp;rsquo ; sake . Questioners need to know all the details before deciding to go along with something &amp;mdash ; the who , what , where , when and why . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Finally , rebels resist both inner and outer expectations . As the smallest percentage of the population , they value authenticity and self-determination above all else . Ask them to do something , and they&amp;rsquo ; ll likely push back . But show them how something falls in line with their identity , and they&amp;rsquo ; ll be more enthusiastic . Think Polonius in Hamlet : &amp;ldquo ; To thine own self be true . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are tricks to implementing happy habits , though , that work for all the tendencies . The &amp;ldquo ; clean slate&amp;rdquo ; approach advises you form new habits when you&amp;rsquo ; re already transitioning to something new &amp;mdash ; like moving to a new house . You can also pair a new habit ( like walking on a treadmill ) with something you already like to do ( like binging Netflix ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Rubin also praises the convenience factor , explaining that we tend to avoid doing something if it&amp;rsquo ; s a hassle . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re wired to look for the shortcut . Every little bit of friction matters . But we can harness this to our advantage , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; On the one hand , it&amp;rsquo ; s like , well , are we lazy ? On the other hand , you&amp;rsquo ; re like , well , I can&amp;rsquo ; t be bothered to get the cookies off the high shelf in the kitchen . It&amp;rsquo ; s a laziness that&amp;rsquo ; s helpful , if it is indeed lazy . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Overall , Rubin is optimistic about us poor , tired , huddled masses and our capacity to change ourselves and our world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think research says people generally are happier across time , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; Probably for each person it&amp;rsquo ; s an individual thing , though . It&amp;rsquo ; s where you are in life , what stage you&amp;rsquo ; re in , challenges you&amp;rsquo ; re facing . Darlings , an ambiguous tale of motherhood , strikes spooky notehttp : **36;3334;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **34;3372;TOOLONG ... title= " Melanie Golding 's debut novel focuses on the darker side of motherhood " alt= " Melanie Golding 's debut novel focuses on the darker side of motherhood " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;3408;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 832906 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Little Darlings&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Melanie Golding&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Harper Collins&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " color : #808000 ; " &gt;&lt;strong&gt;Jamie **35;3438;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; LONDON &amp;mdash ; The opening chapter gets your attention . A distraught woman is at water&amp;rsquo ; s edge , on the verge of plunging her two children into a reservoir in England&amp;rsquo ; s mysterious Peak District . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But then Melanie Golding&amp;rsquo ; s debut novel , Little Darlings , goes backward in time to tell us about the sinister events that have brought a caring young mother to this point . Events that are not quite of this world &amp;ndash ; Kirkus Reviews , an influential organ of the book trade , calls Little Darlings &amp;ldquo ; a gorgeous , creepy , modern fairy tale&amp;rdquo ; that &amp;ldquo ; will strike true fear into the heart of every parent . &amp;rdquo ; Filmmaker Roger Michell , the man who brought Notting Hill to cinemas , was so knocked out by it that he went after the movie rights early on and was hard at work on a screenplay even before the novel&amp;rsquo ; s publication this month . As for the book&amp;rsquo ; s 40-year-old author &amp;mdash ; well , she&amp;rsquo ; s wondering exactly what forces she has set loose in writing it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some of those forces possibly lurk in the spooky preambles that precede each chapter . Such as this piece of advice from Irish &lt;br&gt; folklore : &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; A branch of mountain ash tied over the cradle protects girls against fairy abduction , as according to ancient superstition the first woman was created from the mountain ash . A branch of the alder tree protects boys , as the first man was created from the alder tree . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the novel , published in Canada by HarperCollins , a new mother becomes convinced that her twin boys are not her own &amp;mdash ; that something unspeakable has occurred in the maternity ward when a grotesque woman makes an unearthly appearance and gleefully hisses , &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; ll take yours and you can have mine . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;3475;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;3511;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 832909 " /&gt; Is this an anxious young mother&amp;rsquo ; s paranoia ? Or is something more frightening at play here . Early readers appear divided &amp;mdash ; and this pleases the book&amp;rsquo ; s 40-year-old author . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m happy with both reactions , &amp;rdquo ; she tells Postmedia. &amp;ldquo ; I would like two different people to finish the book and entirely disagree about what really happened . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And if those very ambiguities prove frightening in themselves , that will make Golding happy too because of her own fascination for the inexplicable in folklore , fairy tales , the supernatural and things that go bump in the night . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; People read horror stories to make frightening things safe , &amp;rdquo ; she says matter-of-factly . That&amp;rsquo ; s what fairy tales do too . &amp;rdquo ; Golding cites the brilliant fiction of the late Angela Carter who won widespread praise for her revisionist and often blood-splashed reworkings of the fairy-tale tradition . &amp;ldquo ; And I believe in the power of that tradition &amp;mdash ; yes , &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But what sort of power do they exercise on the life of Lauren Tranter , the central figure in Little Darlings ? Whatever else , she is undeniably a young mother in distress &amp;mdash ; one early review suggested that Little Darlings contains one of the most searing accounts of childbirth and postpartum depression ever set on paper . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I read widely but I don&amp;rsquo ; t think I ever found a realistic account of what having a baby was like , &amp;rdquo ; Golding says . She describes her own experience of childbirth as &amp;ldquo ; traumatic&amp;rdquo ; and suggests that a lot of mothers are &amp;ldquo ; not diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder when they should be . &amp;rdquo ; But , she adds , this does not deny the reality of postnatal depression as well . That condition is present in spades in Little Darlings as Lauren copes with lack of sleep , painful breast-feeding , frightening thoughts and a husband insensitive to her emotional fragility. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On top of all this there&amp;rsquo ; s another sighting of that strange and frightening woman &amp;mdash ; this time outside the family home . Then comes a terrifying event in the park and the disappearance and recovery of the children . That&amp;rsquo ; s when Lauren becomes seriously convinced they are not her own . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Changeling stories show up in virtually every culture , &amp;rdquo ; Golding points out . &amp;ldquo ; And I found that in many cases they are related to the mother having a &amp;lsquo ; mental health&amp;rsquo ; event . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But is Lauren simply hallucinating ? There&amp;rsquo ; s no clear answer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; She questions her sanity quite a bit , &amp;rdquo ; Golding concedes. &amp;ldquo ; But someone once wrote that you only truly lose your sanity when you do stop questioning yourself . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; So again the reader is left with ambiguity and uncertainty &amp;mdash ; and it&amp;rsquo ; s creepy . Golding wanted to have the same chilling effect on the reader as Henry James&amp;rsquo ; s classic ghost story , The Turn Of The Screw . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There&amp;rsquo ; s so much ambiguity in that book , &amp;rdquo ; she says admiringly. &amp;ldquo ; Almost every line of it can be interpreted in more than one way . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She began writing the novel as part of her Master&amp;rsquo ; s course in creative writing at Bath Spa University . She didn&amp;rsquo ; t think she was writing a thriller at the time , but realizes now that those elements are present &amp;mdash ; she does succeed in keeping readers on the edge . At the same time , however , she was also anxious to create a genuinely human document . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; One point of the story is that everything Lauren was before she had a baby is kind of gone . Her old life as an artist and sculptor is gone . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Since the babies arrived she&amp;rsquo ; s seen in a new role &amp;mdash ; as the mother of twins . That&amp;rsquo ; s all she is now , and that&amp;rsquo ; s contributed to her mental state as well . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A further problem is husband Patrick , who&amp;rsquo ; s scarcely a tower of strength in her hour of need . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Patrick&amp;rsquo ; s behaviour is terrible , &amp;rdquo ; Golding says bluntly. &amp;ldquo ; He&amp;rsquo ; s not a good man . Early reviewers absolutely hate him &amp;mdash ; but that&amp;rsquo ; s fine . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; You&amp;rsquo ; re not supposed to like him . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But you do have permission to like Joanna Harper , the caring cop who enters Lauren&amp;rsquo ; s life . In creating her , Golding came to like Jo so much that she&amp;rsquo ; s in her next book as well . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; By the time she started writing Little Darlings , Golding had long been active in the world of music . She was a musician and songwriter and her husband a classical singer . And despite the horrors that Lauren goes through , she likes kids . Not just her own two , now aged seven and nine , but also the many she and her husband came to know at an earlier time when they worked as child minders . &amp;ldquo ; We looked after other people&amp;rsquo ; s kids &amp;mdash ; sort of professional nannies. &amp;rdquo ; And now she runs a weekly &amp;ldquo ; baby toddlers music group&amp;rdquo ; in the Gloucestershire town where she lives . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Mothers come along with their babies and we read stories and sing songs that I&amp;rsquo ; ve written about what happens in the story . In fact , the 10 trees on my block are a spindly bunch , set in small patches of dirt within the sidewalks . A couple of weeks ago I finally noticed that other trees in the area have sprouted green leaves again . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Recent rains no doubt helped . I know , after reading Pamela Hickman&amp;rsquo ; s non-fiction book Trees , that the extra moisture was sucked up by the roots and sent via trunk and branches to the existing but largely unseen buds , &amp;ldquo ; causing them to swell and eventually burst open . &amp;rdquo ; I also learned why the resulting leaves look green : It&amp;rsquo ; s thanks to a chemical called chlorophyll in the leaves . When sunlight hits a leaf , chlorophyll absorbs the red and blue light &amp;ldquo ; but reflects the green part of the spectrum . You see the reflected light , making the leaf appear green&amp;rdquo ; in spring . The leaves contain other colours as well , but they don&amp;rsquo ; t show until fall , when leaves stop making chlorophyll . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This latest addition to Hickman&amp;rsquo ; s Nature All Around series invites kids to arm themselves with notebook and pencil and head out in their neighbourhoods to do some tree-watching . Watercolour and gouache paintings by Carolyn Gavin , a native of South Africa now living in Toronto , can guide the children&amp;rsquo ; s eyes . For ages 6 to 9. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Me , Toma and the Concrete Garden , by Toronto&amp;rsquo ; s Andrew Larsen , takes a non-fiction approach to the outdoors , focusing on the urban landscape . It&amp;rsquo ; s the story of Vincent , a young boy who is sent to spend summer months with his Aunt Mimi while his mother recovers from surgery . The opening two-page spread , illustrated by Montreal&amp;rsquo ; s Anne Villeneuve , shows the densely residential neighbourhood in which Mimi lives , with walk-up apartment buildings surrounding a neglected fenced-in empty lot . The only bits of cheerful colour in the illustration come from a striped umbrella on Aunt Mimi&amp;rsquo ; s balcony and a tasty-looking cone painted on the ice cream truck parked outside the apartment complex . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Vincent makes himself at home with his aunt , but it isn&amp;rsquo ; t until he meets another boy , Toma , near the empty lot that readers get caught up in the action . Aunt Mimi&amp;rsquo ; s balcony contains a box full of &amp;ldquo ; dirt balls&amp;rdquo ; that she received from a secret admirer . &amp;ldquo ; I was hoping they&amp;rsquo ; d be chocolates , &amp;rdquo ; she tells her nephew when he asks about them , adding that she doesn&amp;rsquo ; t know what to do with them . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But Vincent knows . He brings an armload to the boy bouncing a ball against the wall at the empty lot , and suggests they fling them over the fence . Toma agrees , and the two start tossing the dirt balls &amp;mdash ; incurring the wrath of a man on a nearby balcony , someone they call Mr. Grumpypants . His balcony is covered in plants , and it doesn&amp;rsquo ; t take the reader long to figure out that he is likely Aunt Mimi&amp;rsquo ; s secret admirer &amp;ndash ; especially when a few rainy days show that the dirt balls had more than just dirt in them and a colourful inner city garden starts sprouting in the empty lot . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A charming story , wonderfully illustrated , will show urban kids that even the most neglected piece of land can be turned into an eye-catching neighbourhood garden . Gavriel Kay 's A Brightness Long Ago delves into fantasy , mythhttp : **36;3806;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **34;3844;TOOLONG ... title= " " I 've had such good fortune , " says Guy Gavriel Kay " alt= " " I 've had such good fortune , " says Guy Gavriel Kay " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;3880;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 831666 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;A Brightness Long Ago&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Guy Gavriel Kay&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Penguin Random House Canada&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " color : #808000 ; " &gt;&lt;strong&gt;Jamie **35;3910;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; TORONTO &amp;mdash ; Guy Gavriel Kay is chatting about how to activate a curse : You must carve a &amp;ldquo ; curse tablet&amp;rdquo ; in wax and , after baking and hardening it , cast it into the grave of someone newly dead . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He learned about this while researching the culture of sixth-century Byzantium for his bestselling pair of novels known collectively as The Sarantine Mosaic . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A moment later , he&amp;rsquo ; s matter-of-factly talking about &amp;ldquo ; the ancient Chinese belief that unburied ghosts haunt the place where they died . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And then of course there&amp;rsquo ; s that moment in Kay&amp;rsquo ; s latest novel when a dead woman contemplates her own mortality . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Grist for the mill of the fantasy writer ? Well , yes , but there&amp;rsquo ; s a complicating factor when it comes to trying to place Kay in that niche . He doesn&amp;rsquo ; t quite belong there &amp;mdash ; not when his books are so anchored in history . And not when he believes it imperative for today&amp;rsquo ; s reader to understand that the fantastical was once an accepted component of everyday life . To Shakespeare&amp;rsquo ; s audiences , the witches in Macbeth were not a playwright&amp;rsquo ; s invention but a real possibility . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There&amp;rsquo ; s an almost inevitable tendency in many people to feel whimsical or patronizing or superior about these &amp;lsquo ; silly beliefs&amp;rsquo ; of the past , &amp;rdquo ; he says . ( Kay is charitable enough to refrain from taking a swipe at those among us who shudder when a black cat crosses our path. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; What I want to do is give value to those beliefs , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; If the people I&amp;rsquo ; m writing about thought something was so , I&amp;rsquo ; ll write about it . This is not just playing narrative games &amp;mdash ; it&amp;rsquo ; s to let the reader more fully apprehend the world view of people living it in the past . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Kay &amp;mdash ; whom Time magazine once described as &amp;ldquo ; a global phenomenon&amp;rdquo ; &amp;mdash ; is in his publisher&amp;rsquo ; s office to discuss his latest novel , A Brightness Long Ago . Evoking the high drama of Renaissance Italy , it&amp;rsquo ; s a thundering saga of revenge , retribution and redemption . But a significant portion is also a delicately executed memory piece filtered through the prism of a tailor&amp;rsquo ; s son named Danio Cerra who finds himself plunged into the world of two rival warlords who are headed for a deadly showdown . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; ve never done first-person singular before , &amp;rdquo ; Kay says , and he sounds a bit surprised over having done so . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; My cranky old agent says that this may be my most elegiac book , &amp;rdquo ; he says , again with some wonderment. &amp;ldquo ; But I resist the idea that it&amp;rsquo ; s because I&amp;rsquo ; m getting old . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On the contrary , he says , it has to do with continuing artistic growth . &amp;ldquo ; If you&amp;rsquo ; re only interested in the same things at 60 that you were at 30 , you haven&amp;rsquo ; t grown . If you&amp;rsquo ; re an artist and serious about it , there should be changes . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In conversation , Kay reveals an intriguing capacity for self-examination . For example &amp;mdash ; his refusal to prepare an outline before he begins one of his intricately plotted novels . He prefers the excitement of &amp;ldquo ; discovering&amp;rdquo ; where the book wants to go . &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m like Graham Greene , who once said , &amp;lsquo ; I never outline , because if I know where the book is going , I get bored writing it . &amp;rsquo ; &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Kay also wants to make one thing clear about the riveting opening chapter of his new novel . It deals with the bloody disposal of a monstrous sexual predator known as The Beast . &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s tailor-made for the #MeToo and post-Harvey Weinstein era , &amp;rdquo ; he says , &amp;ldquo ; but I will tell you that I wrote that opening eight months before all those stories started breaking . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There&amp;rsquo ; s also the mixture of discomfort and weary resignation he shows over being placed in the &amp;ldquo ; fantasy&amp;rdquo ; genre &amp;mdash ; a designation dating back to his triumphant debut at the age of 29 with The Summer Tree , a mythic spellbinder that was the first volume in a much-loved trilogy , The Fionavar Tapestry . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;3947;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;3983;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 831670 " /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; You&amp;rsquo ; re putting your finger on some of the most challenging , interesting , difficult aspects of my having been a stubborn Prairie kid all my life , &amp;rdquo ; says Kay , who was born in southern Saskatchewan and grew up in Winnipeg . &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re a categorizing species &amp;hellip ; and I&amp;rsquo ; m difficult to categorize . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If you begin in a certain genre and achieve recognition and some degree of prominence in it , &amp;rdquo ; he says , &amp;ldquo ; the odds are that unless you go wildly away from it , that will continue to be how you&amp;rsquo ; re perceived . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; His frustration is understandable . After that career-making trilogy , Kay embarked on his own highly individualistic path , immersing himself in history to create parallel fictional universes for Byzantium , China&amp;rsquo ; s Tang Dynasty and Islamic Spain . In the case of this new novel , A Brightness Long Ago , his inspiration is the turbulence of early Renaissance Italy , its city states and warlords . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Fellow novelist Robert Wiersema once defined Kay&amp;rsquo ; s uniqueness this way : He specialized in &amp;ldquo ; history with a quarter turn . &amp;rdquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s a phrase that Kay embraces . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m not doing straight historical fiction , &amp;rdquo ; he says . Yet his novels are steeped in history , reflecting Kay&amp;rsquo ; s own particular quest for truth . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I don&amp;rsquo ; t want to write a book in which I suggest to the reader that I know Henry Vlll&amp;rsquo ; s favourite position in bed or what Justinian and Theodora&amp;rsquo ; s relationship was like when no one else was in the room with them , &amp;rdquo ; Kay says . His method is to write a novel in which the world of Byzantium becomes the world of Sarantium or in which the city states of Renaissance Italy can be reimagined as Firenta , Mylasia and Seressa . In that way he and the reader enter a shared relationship : &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re inventing the freedom and moral comfort for me of not having to impose thoughts and feelings on real , historical people . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the latest novel , his fictional characters achieve their own focused reality in a world where such disparate events as a bloody assassination and a fixed horse race provide stunning commentaries on the power politics of the time . The two warlords , Teobaldo and Folco , driven by their hatred for each other , are memorable presences , but so are other members of Kay&amp;rsquo ; s gallery &amp;mdash ; among them a strange and enigmatic female healer named Jelana and a young woman of courage and tenacity named Adria. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Kay is a greying 64 now . Yet there&amp;rsquo ; s still a boyish enthusiasm when he talks about his work . Tolkien&amp;rsquo ; s son , Christopher , in editing The Silmarillion , his late father&amp;rsquo ; s monumental history of Middle-earth. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Archival exposure to the Tolkien world had a huge impact on Kay . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I learned some really important things , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; I learned patience . Tolkien was inexhaustibly slow and patient in developing his narratives . Eighteen months of intense reading were required before he felt ready to start A Brightness Long Ago . And as he presides over its launching , his prime emotion is gratitude. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; ve had such good fortune &amp;mdash ; this stubborn Prairie kid being allowed to write in a way that doesn&amp;rsquo ; t fit into boxes , slots , categories in any convenient way &amp;hellip ; to be published around the world while being allowed to write the books I want to write at the speed at which I want to write them . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; For 35 years that&amp;rsquo ; s been a gift from my readers . Coconut Dreams transcends culture , Red Ryan hides a secrethttp : **34;4060;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **34;4096;TOOLONG ... title= " Derek Mascarenhas " alt= " Derek Mascarenhas " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;4132;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 831409 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Coconut Dreams&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Derek **26;4162;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Book*hug Press&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; An epic work in short-story form , Derek Mascarenhas&amp;rsquo ; Coconut Dreams transcends space , time and culture in 10 interconnected tales revolving around two generations of the fictional Pinto family . The book opens with a fable-like story recounting the birth of Felix Pinto and a hair-raising adventure that pits him and his childhood friend Clara against a trio of adult villains in Goa , India . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;4190;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;4226;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 831302 " /&gt; Flash forward 48 years , and we meet Felix and Clara&amp;rsquo ; s children , son Aiden and daughter Ally , as they experience the universal joys and terrors of a suburban childhood a world away , in Burlington , Ont . Snow days and schoolyard bullies , newspaper routes and free-range escapades &amp;mdash ; it&amp;rsquo ; s typical Canadian coming-of-age territory . Except when it&amp;rsquo ; s not . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Along with field trips and first kisses , subtle racism creeps in , with one overt threat that ends in violence . McEwan talks new book Machines Like Mehttp : **38;4584;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **34;4624;TOOLONG ... title= " Author Ian McEwan. " alt= " Author Ian McEwan. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;4660;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 829953 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Machines Like Me&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Ian McEwan&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Penguin Random House Canada&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " color : #808000 ; " &gt;&lt;strong&gt;Eric **35;4690;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Occasionally , Ian McEwan will be asked what he does for a living . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The question might come from a cab driver or someone else he has come across during in his day-to-day life . Sometimes he will simply lie and say he&amp;rsquo ; s an accountant &amp;ldquo ; just to close the question down , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But other times , when he&amp;rsquo ; s in the mood , he will admit to being a writer . That inevitably leads to the next question : What do you write about ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I say : &amp;lsquo ; I write about love , music , physics , math , history &amp;mdash ; &amp;rsquo ; &amp;rdquo ; McEwan says with a laugh , in an interview with Postmedia from his home in London , England . &amp;ldquo ; That&amp;rsquo ; s not a helpful line at all , but it certainly closes the conversation down . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The line may not be helpful , but it is true . McEwan is one of modern fiction&amp;rsquo ; s most beloved and acclaimed storytellers , but it is still difficult to summarize what exactly it is he writes about when looking at his 45-year body of work . It has ranged from his sprawling generation-spanning 2001 classic Atonement to 2016&amp;rsquo ; s Nutshell , a modern-day retelling of Hamlet through the point of view of a fetus . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Even summarizing a single novel by McEwan can prove difficult . Which brings us to his latest , the intriguingly mind-bending , poignant and funny Machines Like Me . It&amp;rsquo ; s a multi-layered tale that involves most of the above areas of interest . That includes a strange love triangle . Science and math play a role since McEwan is speculating on the ramifications of as-yet unrealized advances in artificial intelligence . It also takes place in 1980s London , albeit an alternative history in which England lost the Falklands War , Margaret Thatcher is fighting a losing battle for power against Tony Benn and Alan Turing didn&amp;rsquo ; t commit suicide in 1954 but instead has gone on to become a celebrity scientist and gay icon who helps create synthetic humans . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s such an exhilarating mishmash of ideas that it&amp;rsquo ; s hard to know where to start in speaking with the author . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It turns out , the complexities of the tale have been building piece by piece in his mind since his university days in the late-1960s , even if he didn&amp;rsquo ; t realize it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;4727;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;4763;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 829956 " /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s odd how these things can be lying around in your mind and you don&amp;rsquo ; t even think about writing a novel about them , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; They are just part of the white noise of your own thoughts . It&amp;rsquo ; s almost invisible to you . I&amp;rsquo ; m just impelled to these kind of topics . Suddenly I thought I wanted to write a novel about it . It all started to cohere . Partly because I think it has pressed in on the culture quite strongly with the developments in software in the last few years . I&amp;rsquo ; ve always had an interest in science anyway . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the University of Sussex , McEwan became fascinated by a course he took on the so-called mind-body problem and particularly the questions it posed about whether a machine could think . In the late-1970s , he wrote The Imitation Game , a Second World War TV drama partly set at Bletchley Park . That was the secret facility where Turing made his codebreaking breakthroughs and became the forefather of computer science . ( Although it has the same title and some similar subject matter , McEwan&amp;rsquo ; s story is not the basis for the 2014 movie starring Benedict Cumberbatch as Turing. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Around the same time , McEwan was moonlighting as a feature journalist and one of his assignments was to interview a professor of robotics at the University of Edinburgh , who also happened to be at Bletchley Park during Turing&amp;rsquo ; s heyday . Later , McEwan began following the work of his friend Daniel Dennett and other philosophers , becoming particularly fascinated with an area of study in the 1990s that looked at the relationship between consciousness and neuroscience. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; These things have been in my mind a long time , &amp;rdquo ; McEwan says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the heart of Machines Like Me is a love triangle between a drifting would-be intellectual named Charlie , his young&amp;nbsp ; but mysterious neighbour and girlfriend Miranda and a synthetic human named Adam . In this alternate universe , much of the technology we have today exists as of 1982 thanks in part to Turing , who has also overseen advancements in artificial intelligence that far exceed what we have today . Adam is an intriguing creation . He is potentially lethal , at times insufferably moralistic but deeply in love with Miranda and prone to writing endless haiku poems in her honour . But he also has knowledge of a dark secret in her past of which Charlie is not initially aware . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Because England lost the Falklands War , London circa the 1980s makes for a chaotic backdrop full of unemployment , political upheaval and rioting . But McEwan says setting the tale in an alternate 1980s was more practical than anything else . He didn&amp;rsquo ; t want to write a science-fiction novel set in the future and he needed a time when Turing could still be alive . In real life , Turing was charged with indecency in 1952 under England&amp;rsquo ; s anti-homosexuality laws . Rather than face imprisonment , he chose to undergo brutal hormonal treatment . He committed suicide a few years later . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Like so much of Machines Like Me , the character of Turing was based on a simple what-if scenario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; He could easily have gone down another route , &amp;rdquo ; McEwan says . &amp;ldquo ; Imagining ( him as a ) rather chubby , conventionally dressed man who would have confronted the &amp;rsquo ; 60s in a decade , that experience became a sort of puzzle . What would his life have been like ? Would he have been altered profoundly by the 1960s ? Would he have come out as gay ? Would he have become a figure , a symbol , an icon ? Might he , in his brilliance , become a figure in the culture like Einstein was or Stephen Hawking ? It&amp;rsquo ; s almost like sending a letter back to him saying how I wish you had lived . How I wish you had lived where you could have been openly gay and proud of it and useful to others . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The novel explores heady themes of consciousness and humanity and how history is contingent on a mix of events , choices and chance that could easily have gone differently and led to a significantly altered present . &amp;nbsp ; It&amp;rsquo ; s trippy stuff . But McEwan says the real core of book is a moral dilemma that Charlie , Miranda and Adam eventually face and come to opposite decisions about . This may prove to be the most controversial aspect of the novel , particularly in the context of the #Metoo movement . We discover that Miranda&amp;rsquo ; s past involves a sexual assault and a trial . While it would be a spoiler to give too much away , the situation poses unsettling questions about justice , revenge , morality and truth . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; McEwan acknowledges the #Metoo movement means Machines Like Me will be emerging into a culture much different from the one in which even 2001&amp;rsquo ; s Atonement was released . Among other things , Atonement explored the long-term ramifications of a false accusation of sexual assault &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But the author says the sexual assault aspect in this novel serves a specific purpose in the plot . He wasn&amp;rsquo ; t thinking about the #Metoo movement at all . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I was looking for a dilemma and one that was really strong . Not just a minor fact , but one where a life was involved and a terrible cruelty , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; Adam takes one view , which is also Turing&amp;rsquo ; s view , and Charlie and Miranda take another . I was trying to get it so that people would feel genuinely split , not among themselves but within themselves . That&amp;rsquo ; s really the heart of the matter . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As for any other similarities or thematic threads between Atonement and Machines Like Me , or between any of his novels , McEwan says he will leave that for others to find . At 70 , he admits he doesn&amp;rsquo ; t give much thought to his body of work as a whole . Recently , his publisher sent him new paperback editions of all of his books . All of them &amp;mdash ; from his 1978 debut The Cement Garden to 1998&amp;rsquo ; s Man Booker Prize-winning Amsterdam to his critically acclaimed 2014 novel The Children&amp;rsquo ; s Act &amp;mdash ; are currently piled on top of eachother on his filing cabinet . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When I walk past them , there&amp;rsquo ; s a very complicated feeling about it , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; That pile can only get so high . That&amp;rsquo ; s the memento mori feeling about it . How many more have I got ? That&amp;rsquo ; s one thought . The other is , yeah , if I put my finger on the spine of any of those books in this 12-inch pile , I know exactly where I was , what my circumstances were , how life was when I was writing it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; So it is a curious thing . It gives off a sort of radioactive heat . And sometimes I think I ought to put them out of sight . I don&amp;rsquo ; t like being disturbed every time I walk past . Martin 's Press&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " color : #808000 ; " &gt;&lt;strong&gt;Dana **31;5122;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When Irshad Manji began writing her latest book , Don&amp;rsquo ; t Label Me : An Incredible Conversation for Divided Times , she knew she had to take a different approach than she had employed in the past to communicating with those who disagree with her . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; No longer would the outspoken educator , advocate and author of the lightning-rod books The Trouble With Islam Today ( formerly titled The Trouble With Islam ) and Allah , Liberty and Love be a subscriber to the take-no-prisoners approach . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; As a matter of fact , I did have an ah-ha moment , &amp;rdquo ; Manji says . &amp;ldquo ; About three months into the writing of Don&amp;rsquo ; t Label Me , I knew I did not want to lapse into a polemic again . This had to be something more inviting than a rant . I was frankly beginning to slide into my very opinionated way . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Enter Lily , an old deaf and blind **28;5155;TOOLONG rescue dog . Lily was Manji&amp;rsquo ; s first dog , since Manji was raised in a religious Muslim family that believes dogs are evil . &amp;ldquo ; One of the ways we bonded is that I would talk to her about the ideas swimming in my head , &amp;rdquo ; says Manji , who lives in Honolulu with her wife , Laura Albano , and their rescue dogs . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The idea for a new book about true , honest rapport was hatched . In Don&amp;rsquo ; t Label Me , Manji has an imaginary conversation in which Lily asks questions , presses points and is the devil&amp;rsquo ; s advocate that tilts its little dog head while asking Manji , &amp;ldquo ; Really ? &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When I began to write it as a dialogue between myself and Lily , the various pieces of what I wanted to say and how I was wanting to say it fell into place , &amp;rdquo ; says Manji , the founder of the Moral Courage Project . &amp;ldquo ; She plays the role in the book of challenging me at almost every turn . She brought out the internal debate I&amp;rsquo ; m having with myself . I knew if I was writing this as a conversation with Lily that I would never become too harsh in the way I express myself , because I would never become harsh with Lily . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It may seem like a gimmicky construct , but it works as a way for Manji to argue that we need to put aside our tribal tendencies and differences and really talk to the people we don&amp;rsquo ; t agree with . We need to stop vilifying the other side and maybe they won&amp;rsquo ; t retreat and return with radical sentiments that can be found , say , in the white-nationalist movement . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;5185;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;5221;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 829937 " /&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s how to avoid Backlash 101. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Manji&amp;rsquo ; s strategic point in this book is clear and clever &amp;mdash ; and easily doable. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m not asking anybody to compromise or dilute their convictions by listening to people who disagree with them , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; Not at all . What I&amp;rsquo ; m saying is you can both stand your ground and seek common ground so that you can be heard in a way that you wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t have otherwise . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The New York Times bestselling author says the best way to start this approach is the best way to start anything &amp;mdash ; pause and take a breath . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Let&amp;rsquo ; s start with the basics . When you are &amp;mdash ; let&amp;rsquo ; s use a buzzword of the day , triggered &amp;mdash ; by somebody else&amp;rsquo ; s beliefs , first take a breath . Literally just take a breath , because when you do that you are working with your biology , not against it and you&amp;rsquo ; re literally decelerating the blood rush in your body , &amp;rdquo ; says Manji. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; You are slow-jamming the primitive part of your brain . That allows you to , in fact , outwit the impulse to attack and to label . By slowing yourself down just a bit , you are able to tap into the more evolved part of the brain that allows you to make more rational choices . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; By &amp;ldquo ; slow-jamming , &amp;rdquo ; our lizard brains , she says , we are much more able to find a better balance between emoting and contemplating . If you truly listen to what the other person is saying , you are offering up respect , not giving up giving up power . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We first need to remember the basic law of human psychology , which is this : If you want to be heard , you have to first be willing to hear , &amp;rdquo ; says Manji. &amp;ldquo ; The more questions you ask , the more heard they will feel . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The idea of slowing down and taking a breath can also be a simple adjustment that reminds you to not jump to conclusions . Not to hastily attach labels . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For Manji , Lily was an example of the narrow and usually negative conceptions that come with looking at a book and deciding the cover was enough . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Whatever labels other people place on Lily &amp;mdash ; for example , old and blind &amp;mdash ; they would never appreciate her fully if that was all they were going by , &amp;rdquo ; says Manji about her late , great companion . &amp;ldquo ; That again was a core lesson that I tried to impart in the book &amp;mdash ; that if we are really interested in diversity , we won&amp;rsquo ; t reduce people to the labels we have for them . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And , as Manji pointed out on a recent guest spot on the HBO&amp;rsquo ; s political show Real Time with Bill Maher , she herself has been covered with labels . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; So if we know it&amp;rsquo ; s bad , why can&amp;rsquo ; t we stop the impulse to label others ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The brain does need short cuts for the information coming our way , &amp;rdquo ; Manji says . &amp;ldquo ; Of course , the problem with those short cuts and in life itself is that sometimes , and in this case often , shortcuts actually get you more lost than you already feel . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Looking back , Manji wishes she had practised what she is preaching now when she was travelling the world and scorching the earth with her speeches and interviews about the problems she had with the traditional beliefs of Islam . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As a young , gay , female Muslim , she wanted reform . In turn , she became fully loaded and spoiling for a fight . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I wish I had done more of what I am writing about now , &amp;rdquo ; says Manji. &amp;ldquo ; I , too , was far too defensive . Where are you coming from ? &amp;rsquo ; I wish I would have asked those questions instead of merely reacting . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In June 2011 , Manji was in the makeup room at an NBC studio when suddenly she collapsed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That health scare caused her to check in on herself . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It reminded me the world will not stop spinning with or without my voice , &amp;rdquo ; says Manji. &amp;ldquo ; I realized I have to take the burden of winning off my shoulders and just have a conversation . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; While 2019 Manji may be mellower in her approach , she is by no means free of strong opinions . @@51674904 <h> Weather Extremes Are The New Norm For Canadians : Experts <h> " This is the kind of thing people have been predicting for years . " <p> THE CANADIAN PRESS/John WoodsSun Dogs , formed by the sun reflecting off ice crystals in bitterly cold temperatures , sit over the Winnipeg skyline Wednesday , Jan. 30 , 2019 . Winnipeg and the region has been experiencing below -35 degree celsius temperatures and windchills of -45 to -50 degree celsius . <p> As Ottawa limps across the finish line of its snowiest January on record , cherry blossoms are blooming at the legislature in coastal Victoria , B.C. <p> Millions of Canadians were hiding out this week under extreme cold warnings stretching across the map , even as some East Coast cities enjoyed moderate temperatures . <p> This is the kind of thing people have been predicting for years.Konrad Gajewski , University of Ottawa <p> According to experts , these co-existing extremes have been predicted for some time -- and they 're likely here to stay . <p> " This is the kind of thing people have been predicting for years , " said Konrad Gajewski , a professor of geography and environment at the University of Ottawa . <p> " This kind of pattern of more alternation , more extremes , both in terms of warm and cold conditions is what we 're expecting for the future . " <h> Common belief says warming Arctic to blame <p> Central Canada 's cold snap comes from the oscillating upper wind patterns of the jet stream , pushing the cold air down from the north with the polar vortex . <p> At the same time , the large " waves " in the wind patterns push some warm air north , explaining comparatively warm temperatures on the coasts . <p> The exact role climate change plays in the pattern 's changes is an ongoing discussion in the scientific community , but a common belief says it 's the result of a warming Arctic . <p> " It 's thought that as the Arctic warms up because the ice is melting back , we 're going to have more of a situation where you have what we call ' waviness ' in the polar vortex , " Gajewski said . <p> REUTERS/Moe DoironIce and snow cover branches near the brink of the Horseshoe Falls , due to subzero temperatures in Niagara Falls , Jan. 22 , 2019 . <p> This " waviness " in the upper wind 's pattern could be carrying cold further and further south into south and central Canada , and pushing warm air further north along the coast . <p> Atmospheric physics professor Kent Moore at the University of Toronto says the striking weather patterns show how the world 's climate system is intimately coupled , and how changes in the coldest and warmest regions can be felt in central Canadian cities . <p> As an example , Moore pointed to the theory that the waves in upper wind patterns are moving slower , with larger amplitudes as a possible result of warming in the Arctic . <p> " The largest changes in the climate are occurring in the Arctic and some would say , ' Who cares ? I live in mid-latitudes , why should I care about that stuff ? ' " Moore said . <p> " The Earth is kind of a small place and so things that happen in the Arctic do n't stay in the Arctic . " <p> This interconnectedness of the world 's climate system also explains the impacts from El Nino systems on Canada , Moore said . <h> More planning for snow-clearing , flood response needed <p> David Atkinson , a climate professor at the University of Victoria , said the jet stream 's behaviour could also make the increasingly frequent , intense storms on the East Coast gain even more strength . <p> " If the air is kind of moving apart , it allows surface air to rise more easily , " Atkinson said . " That helps a storm to work , storms depend on rising air . " <p> Gajewski said the arrival of long-predicted weather patterns means it 's time for all levels of government to seriously plan for changes that are already hitting Canada in the form of sweltering heat waves in the summer and record cold in the winter . <p> This could mean more snow-clearing and flood response on the municipal level and global warming mitigation efforts across the board . <p> We 're going to have to shovel more often . <p> In Ottawa , Gajewski pointed to some ongoing local efforts like more bicycle lanes and efforts to plow some of them in the winter . <p> " A lot of it would just be common sense . It 's going to get hotter in the summers and we 're going to get perhaps more snow , more rain , more extreme conditions , more floods , " Gajewski said . <p> " Cities have to be planned to deal with that kind of thing . " <p> For cities like Ottawa , which just completed its twelfth straight day of round-the-clock plowing , people should n't plan to retire their shovels any time soon . 
@@51675069 <h> You are here <p> rabble blogs are the personal pages of some of Canada 's most insightful progressive activists and commentators . All opinions belong to the writer ; however , writers are expected to adhere to our guidelines . We welcome new bloggers -- contact us for details . <h> Harper delivers a tough message in the throne speech , then leaves town <p> Keep Karl on Parl ! Donate today to have Parliamentary reporting for the rest of us . <p> The pre-throne speech spin told us that Wednesday 's event would serve to unveil the new , kinder and gentler Conservative government . <p> We are not the big business party , chief Conservative spinner , Industry Minister James Moore told interviewers . We are really the consumers ' party , he said . <p> Well , it seems the spinners and those who drafted the actual speech were not on the same page . <p> The touted consumer stuff is buried deep in the speech and promises very little . There are promises about roaming charges and pick-and-pay cable television , but neither the promised air travellers ' bill of rights nor much that is concrete on bank and credit card charges . <p> No more Mr. Nice Guy <p> In fact , what the speech does emphasize is not the Mr. Nice Guy stuff we were promised . It is , rather , red meat , core conservative stuff . <p> It starts with the promise ( that was pointedly not leaked beforehand ) of balanced budget legislation -- the policy non-sequitur to end all policy non-sequiturs . <p> For critics who might say it is hypocritical for a government that not long ago resorted to massive deficit financing to propose balanced budget legislation , the speech has an important qualification . <p> It states that the proposed legislation would allow for deficits in times of " economic crisis " -- although even in such times there would have to be " concrete timelines for returning to balance . " <p> The speech then goes on to promise to freeze what it calls the " federal operation budget . " The goal of that measure , in case anyone might have missed it , is to " restrain hiring . " <p> The Conservatives still have the public service in their sights , and they want to make that quite clear . <p> In addition to the bit on the operating budget , this speech talks pointedly about increasing " performance accountability " in the public service . It seems that treating its own employees as part of the problem and not an essential element of the solution is becoming a habit with the Harper government . <p> In much the same vein , the speech makes reference to the government 's longstanding efforts to cut so-called " red tape " for businesses . Those over-zealous efforts were , in part , at the root of the much-publicized abuses of the Temporary Foreign Worker Program . The speech claims that the government is still committed to vague reforms in the Temporary Foreign Worker Program . It says that , somehow , Canadians should get the first crack at all jobs . <p> Policies on opposite ends of the spectrum <p> There is one non-partisan , evidence-based , solid policy in the speech : the promise to work with British Columbia and Ontario ( and other willing provinces ) to set up what the speech calls " a cooperative regulatory system for securities and capital markets . " <p> In this world of mega-corporations and monster concentrations of wealth , it makes little sense for a medium-sized economy such as Canada 's to have the fragmented system it has for overseeing and regulating equity markets . <p> There is nothing political or particularly Conservative about this one sane and reasonable idea . <p> It is , indeed , a rare case in which the Harper government 's policy did not emanate from the fevered brains of the political backroom operators . This policy was , in fact , carefully crafted by those professional public servants the Conservatives so love to denigrate and disrespect . <p> At the other end of the spectrum , the single most disingenuous -- in fact , downright dishonest -- statement in the speech harkens back to former Immigration Minister Jason Kenney 's package of refugee reforms , Bill C-31 . The speech actually boasts that those reforms " increased protection for genuine refugees . " <p> The truth is exactly the opposite . <p> Kenney 's reforms created a two-tier system for refugee claimants , depriving many of any realistic chance of proving their case . Kenney also yanked basic and necessary health care away from a large number of asylum seekers in Canada . <p> Conservatives boasted about that latter nasty and gratuitous cut in their fundraising calls to identified core supporters . It is obvious the Harper team thinks there is a market out there for the politics of small-mindedness and resentment . <p> A new trade deal on the horizon <p> The big news that the speech did telegraph is that Canada is very close to reaching a Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement ( CETA ) with the European Union . In fact , on Thursday , the Prime Minster will not attend the first day of Parliament following the throne speech . He will fly to Europe , supposedly to either finalize or sign the agreement . <p> For the Prime Minister to be absent at the very opening of a new session is , at least according to Opposition Leader Tom Mulcair , unprecedented . <p> Harper seems to hope that this new trade deal will help rebrand him and his government . <p> We will soon see what Canadians might have to sacrifice to achieve a trade deal with Europe , if there is indeed a deal . <p> One group that was definitely sacrificed in these negotiations are the central and east European Roma , who for more than a decade have been seeking asylum in Canada , fleeing severe discrimination and neo-Nazi violence . <p> One consequence of the Kenney refugee reforms was to declare virtually all European Union countries to be so-called " safe countries of origin , " a designation that has almost totally cut off the inflow of Roma to Canada . <p> That " safe country " status , with all of its consequences , may not be a written part of any deal Harper could sign , but it was clearly a precondition for a trade agreement -- an agreement that is now a key piece of Harper 's political strategy . <p> Devil in the details : Resource development , First Nations rights and the environment <p> And what about massive resource development plans , the rights of First Nations and the environment ? Those were high on the policy agenda just a few months ago , but the speech has very little to say about them . <p> It makes the vaguest of vague commitments to Aboriginal peoples ' having the " opportunity to benefit " from resource exploitation ; while on the environment Harper shamelessly steals an idea from NDP Leader Mulcair and promises to " enshrine the polluter-pay system into law . " <p> Sounds promising , but in this case , the devil will really be in the details . <p> If you want a better sense of what the Harper government really means when it talks about the environment , you only have to consult what the speech says on climate change policy . <p> Near the end of the hour-long rhetorical exercise , the government promises to " build on its record as the first government to achieve an absolute reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by working with provinces to reduce emissions from the oil and gas sectors , while ensuring Canadian companies remain competitive . " <p> Let 's deconstruct that seemingly anodyne statement . <p> In the first place , the Harper government can not take any credit for Canada 's greenhouse gas reductions . That was all the work of the sluggish economy and the genuine efforts of a number of provinces , including Ontario and Quebec . <p> Then , to say that the government will " build on a record " of non-action -- or of retrograde action that included withdrawing from the Kyoto Accord and backing away from a previous commitment to a cap-and-trade system -- and qualify that " commitment " by pledging to ensure the competitiveness of the oil and gas sector ... well that is an environmental pledge that sounds far more ominous than promising . <p> Law-and-order policies and a seemingly softer side <p> Similarly ominous -- and almost scary -- is the deep red meat , hardcore stuff in the parts of the speech that deal with so-called law-and-order policies . <p> In the speech the Conservatives now pledge to introduce a new life sentence that does not even include the possibility of parole after 25 years . Try telling people who work in corrections that this sort of draconian sentence will make their jobs any easier . Those corrections folks will almost universally admit that prisoners without the slightest hope of ever seeing daylight again have no incentive whatsoever to make an effort to rehabilitate themselves . <p> Harper 's throne speech also tells vulnerable sex workers that the government 's priority will be to uphold the existing prostitution laws ; and it sends a message to drug addicts and those who treat them that the government plans to close what it calls " loopholes that allow for the feeding of addiction under the guise of treatment . " <p> Near the end , in an attempt to shore up the government 's softer side , the speech trots out the Harper government 's oft-repeated commitment ( salutary , as far as it goes ) to maternal and child health in the developing world . <p> This little nod to the softer side is much mitigated , however , by the fact that the government will not fund any organizations that facilitate abortions . And that even includes abortions for young girls who are victims of rape or of those forced marriages the government so vigorously condemns . <p> Somehow the Harper government really thinks it is possible to be against the forced marriages of children , but not in favour of dealing with one of the most obvious and far-reaching consequence of such marriages . <p> More people are reading rabble.ca than ever and unlike many news organizations , we have never put up a paywall -- at rabble we 've always believed in making our reporting and analysis free to all , while striving to make it sustainable as well . Media is n't free to produce . rabble 's total budget is likely less than what big corporate media spend on photocopying ( we kid you not ! ) and we do not have any major foundation , sponsor or angel investor . We live or die on community support -- your support ! We get hundreds of thousands of visitors and we believe in them . We believe in you . Depend on a community of visitors who care passionately about media that amplifies the voices of people struggling for change and justice . It really is that simple . @@51676081 <p> Experts link floods like the one in Brantford , Ont. to climate change . Brantford residents were forced out due to flooding along the Grand River on Wednesday , February 21 , 2018 . THE CANADIAN PRESS/Aaron Vincent Elkaim <p> The Ontario NDP is warning voters against falling for promises that they say roll off the tongue just a little too easy . <p> Since entering provincial politics in January , Progressive Conservative Leader Doug Ford has promised to repeal Ontario 's cap-and-trade system and fight any move by Ottawa to impose a carbon tax in its place . <p> The New Democrats , however , say the Tories ' pledge risks putting taxpayers on the hook for " hundreds of millions or billions " of dollars . <p> I have been very clear , the Ontario PCs will scrap Kathleen Wynne 's expensive cap-and-trade carbon tax scheme . " -- Doug Ford <p> " In both cases we 're talking about parties looking after themselves and not paying attention to the interests of the province as a whole , " Tabuns said . <p> As the NDP 's party 's energy and environment critic , he said Ford has made a commitment " in order to advance his political interest , not actually to look after the people of Ontario . " <p> The Tories are brushing aside any such suggestion . <p> " Ontario families and businesses struggling to keep their head above water ca n't afford a carbon tax . It makes life more expensive , and our province more uncompetitive , " Doug Ford said in an emailed statement . <p> But a Canadian law firm dedicated to climate and clean energy says extricating Ontario from the cap-and-trade market with Quebec and California would be " more than an administrative nightmare " and ushers in more uncertainty for businesses . <p> DeMarco Allan LLP senior partner Lisa DeMarco said it would take years to untangle the agreement , an unknown amount of cash to reimburse companies who have bought into the market , and opens Ontario to lawsuits , especially from companies in California . <p> " It would be very , very difficult , " DeMarco told iPolitics . <p> Carbon pricing supporters largely agree with that assessment , but at least one industry group does not . <p> The Chemistry Industry Association of Canada says companies already lack certainty in the current cap-and-trade system because many of the regulations for the next phase of the market have not been set . <p> " We 're not asking for repeal but neither are we afraid of it , " said the association 's president and CEO Bob Masterson . <p> Ontario 's Environment Minister Chris Ballard has previously dismissed the idea of repealing the cap-and-trade system , but this week acknowledged that " anything is possible . " <h> How Ontario can get out of dodge <p> Brought into force in January , the market with California and Quebec was first announced in 2015 . In Ontario , electricity importers and fuel suppliers are among the companies that are required to take part in the system . <p> The agreement allows for any jurisdiction to pull out of the market , but it sets limits on the timing , meaning even if Ford takes government after the June election , it would be years before Ontario gets out of cap-and-trade . <p> Ontario is expected to give California and Quebec 12 months notice if it wants to bail on the shared carbon market . And it can only leave at the end of a compliance period . The current one wraps up at the end of 2020 . <p> Ontario 's system is aimed at lowering greenhouse gas emissions by putting caps on the amount of pollution companies in certain industries can emit . If they exceed those limits they must buy allowances at quarterly auctions or from other companies that come in under their limits . <p> The province has raised nearly $2.5 billion so far from the auctions and its already allocated close to $2 billion of that for spending on green initiatives like home retrofits and transportation projects . <h> Reimbursing companies <p> DeMarco said that in the event of Ontario pulling out of the scheme , the government would have to figure out how to " reverse engineer " the six auctions that have already happened and figure out whether companies need to be refunded for buying emissions allowances . <p> To further complicate matters , she said Ontario would n't just have to worry about its own companies but also those in Quebec and California that have bought or sold allowances in this province . <p> " It would be quite challenging , " she said . " If you just take the time it 's taken to create the system and reverse it then yeah , I think you 're looking at years . " <p> Ontario 's environment department says its already started selling emissions allowances for the compliance period that will start in 2021 . Of the 131,338,242 allowances sold so far , it said 8,576,000 are for the period after 2020 . <p> Whether the province would refund those purchases -- and at what cost -- is a big unknown , according to DeMarco , who pointed out that companies only bought into them because they were required to . <p> But Masterson said he believed that most companies would n't need to be refunded because they were purchasing allowances for the period ending in 2020 . <p> " You ca n't make the assumption that every entity that ever bought an allowance is going to come back and ask for a rebate , " he said . <h> Heading for the courts <p> DeMarco said walking out of the cap-and-trade market would likely also come with " legal consequences " especially because California is part of the equation . <p> She points out that while the system was a cost to some companies , it was a money-maker for others . The big difference between cap-and-trade and carbon tax is that companies can create " value from it . " <p> " In cap-and-trade you can do more than you are required to do and sell the excess for value , " she explains . <p> In the face of regulatory changes , DeMarco said American companies are " much more litigious than Canadians are , " meaning that Ontario risks entering a legal quagmire . <p> " American companies are much more likely to sue , " she said . " They regularly take their government to court , we do n't do that very often as Canadian companies . " <p> Ford is promising to join Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe in fighting any carbon tax that Ottawa plans to impose on provinces that do n't implement their own carbon price . He has said he will go " all the way to the Supreme Court if we have to , if it means stopping this tax from being rammed down our province 's throats . " <p> Ottawa has already tabled legislation that would impose a price on carbon on the provinces . DeMarco said Ontario would end up with a more expensive system if the province trades in the current system for one from the Trudeau Liberals . <p> The Progressive Conservatives have said they do n't plan to release a full platform , but rather focus on a few policy planks . It 's not clear if the plan for exiting the cap-and-trade market will be part of that . 
@@51676487 <p> Canada 's fall election is in full swing and climate policy will likely be at the centre of debate . Prime Minister Justin Trudeau 's Liberals are trumpeting their carbon pricing policy , while Andrew Scheer 's Conservatives want to get rid of it . Meanwhile , Elizabeth May and her newly relevant Greens think Canada must do more to manage the climate crisis . <p> But where do Canadian voters stand on this issue ? <p> Our research team , based at the Universit ? de Montr ? al and the University of California Santa Barbara , has new public opinion data to answer this question . Using recent statistical and political science advances , we can estimate Canadian opinion in every single riding across the country ( except for the less densely populated territories , where data collection is sparse ) . And we 've released on online tool so anyone can see how their local riding compares to others across the country . <p> Canadians are concerned about climate change <p> Our results reinforce what is increasingly clear : climate change is on the minds of Canadians , and not just in urban or coastal communities . A majority of Canadians in every single riding believe the climate is changing . The highest beliefs are in Halifax , where 93 per cent of the public believe climate change is happening . <p> Percentage of Canadians , by riding , who believe climate change is happening . Author provided <p> And a majority of Canadians in all but three ridings think their province has already experienced the impacts of climate change . These beliefs are particularly high in Qu ? bec , where 79 per cent feel the impacts of climate change have already arrived . <p> Canadians also want to see the government take the climate threat seriously . <p> A majority of voters supports emissions trading . Carbon taxation is more divisive , yet more people support carbon taxation than do n't in 88 per cent of Canadian ridings . <p> And the handful of ridings that do n't support the Trudeau government 's carbon pricing policy -- Fort McMurray-Cold Lake , for example -- are already in Conservative hands . <p> In other words , the path to a majority government -- or even a minority government -- goes through many ridings where Canadians are worried about climate change and want the government to take aggressive action . <p> Compared to the United States , the Canadian public believes climate change is happening in far higher shares . Even Canadian ridings where belief in climate change is the lowest have comparable beliefs to liberal states like Vermont and Washington . Overall Canadian support for a carbon tax is higher than support for a carbon tax in California , often thought of as the most environmentally progressive U.S. state . <p> Percentage of Canadians , by riding , who believe their province has already been impacted by climate change . Author provided <p> Importantly , support for specific climate policies remains high in provinces that have already implemented climate laws . For instance , support for a carbon tax in British Columbia , where this policy was introduced in 2008 , is the second highest in the country at 61 per cent ( Prince Edward Island has the highest support ) . Similarly , support for emissions trading is second highest in Qu ? bec , again just behind P.E.I. , where a carbon market was implemented in 2013 . <p> Even Conservative ridings want action <p> We do n't find evidence of a backlash to carbon taxes or emissions trading -- Canadians living in provinces with substantive climate policies continue to support them . Instead , we find substantial support for climate action in the ridings of Canadian politicians who have done the most to undermine Canada 's climate policy . <p> Ontario Premier Doug Ford 's provincial riding matches up with the federal riding of Etobicoke North , where 62 per cent of the public supports emissions trading . In other words , Ford ignored the majority will of his own constituents when he acted to repeal Ontario 's policy last year . <p> Riding-level public opinion estimates for the Saskatchewan riding of Regina-Qu'Apelle , currently represented by Conservative Leader Andrew Scheer . Author provided <p> The same is true federally . In Scheer 's own riding of Regina-Qu'Appelle , support for carbon taxation is at 52 per cent . Only 41 per cent of Scheer 's own constituents oppose a carbon tax . He too is offside with the people he represents . <p> The political risks of opposing climate reforms <p> Our results emphasize how the media can sometimes misinterpret electoral mandates . In Ontario , Doug Ford promised to repeal the province 's emissions trading scheme -- and won .
